title: EDL
description: The deterministic edit plan for one video output. Every creative decision in the finished film or reel is expressed here; the renderer executes it and decides nothing.
$comment:
=====================================================================
 OPENTIMELINEIO MAPPING -- READ BEFORE CHANGING ANY FIELD IN THIS FILE
=====================================================================

 Requirement: an EDL must be losslessly exportable to OpenTimelineIO, so a
 pro user can open our auto-cut in Resolve or Premiere and finish it by hand.
 'Losslessly' here means: export to .otio, re-import, and get a byte-identical
 EDL back. Two rules make that achievable.

 RULE 1 -- Structure maps onto OTIO natives, never onto metadata.
 Anything OTIO models natively (clips, gaps, transitions, time, speed,
 markers, media references) uses the OTIO shape exactly, including its
 half-open TimeRange convention and its RationalTime value/rate pair. This is
 why nothing in this contract stores seconds as a float: 30000/1001 has no
 float representation that survives a round trip, and a drifting frame is a
 missed beat.

 RULE 2 -- Everything else round-trips through one metadata namespace.
 Beat grids, story arcs, reframe keyframe tracks and ducking rules have no
 OTIO equivalent. They are written into the OTIO `metadata` dict under the
 single key "memory_engine", which OTIO preserves verbatim across read/write
 and which every NLE ignores safely. An importer reconstructs the EDL from
 that namespace; an editor who never looks at it still gets a correct cut.

 FIELD-BY-FIELD MAPPING

 EDL                          -> otio.schema.Timeline
  .name                       ->   Timeline.name
  .global_start_time          ->   Timeline.global_start_time (RationalTime)
  .tracks[]                   ->   Timeline.tracks (a Stack of Tracks)
  .story_arc                  ->   Timeline.metadata.memory_engine.story_arc
                                   (+ one Marker per act on the arc track,
                                    for editor visibility only -- the
                                    authoritative copy is the metadata)
  .beat_grid                  ->   Timeline.metadata.memory_engine.beat_grid
                                   (+ one Marker per downbeat, same rule)
  .audio_plan.ducking         ->   Timeline.metadata.memory_engine.ducking
  .audio_plan.mix             ->   Timeline.metadata.memory_engine.mix
  .reframe_tracks[]           ->   Timeline.metadata.memory_engine.reframe_tracks
  .determinism                ->   Timeline.metadata.memory_engine.determinism
  .variant                    ->   Timeline.metadata.memory_engine.variant
  .target                     ->   Timeline.metadata.memory_engine.target

 Track                        -> otio.schema.Track
  .kind                       ->   Track.kind ("Video" | "Audio")
  .name                       ->   Track.name
  .items[]                    ->   Track (children list, in order)

 Clip (item_type="clip")      -> otio.schema.Clip
  .name                       ->   Clip.name
  .source_range               ->   Clip.source_range (TimeRange, half-open)
  .media_ref_id -> MediaRef   ->   Clip.media_reference (ExternalReference)
  .enabled                    ->   Clip.enabled
  .markers[]                  ->   Clip.markers[] (otio.schema.Marker)
  .time_effect (linear_speed) ->   Clip.effects += otio.schema.LinearTimeWarp
                                     (time_scalar)
  .time_effect (freeze)       ->   Clip.effects += otio.schema.FreezeFrame
  .color_ops[]                ->   Clip.effects += otio.schema.Effect with
                                     effect_name "memory_engine.color" and the
                                     op in its metadata
  .moment_id, .beat_lock,
  .reframe_track_id,
  .source_media_id            ->   Clip.metadata.memory_engine.*

 Gap (item_type="gap")        -> otio.schema.Gap
  .duration                   ->   Gap.source_range.duration

 Transition                   -> otio.schema.Transition
  (item_type="transition")
  .transition_type            ->   Transition.transition_type
                                   ("SMPTE_Dissolve" | "Custom")
  .in_offset                  ->   Transition.in_offset
  .out_offset                 ->   Transition.out_offset
  .easing                     ->   Transition.metadata.memory_engine.easing

 MediaRef                     -> otio.schema.ExternalReference
  .available_range            ->   ExternalReference.available_range
  .member_media_ids,
  .continuity,
  .color_encoding,
  .source_peak_nits           ->   ExternalReference.metadata.memory_engine.*
                                   (no OTIO native carries any of them, and a
                                    round trip that drops them loses the member
                                    ORDER the assembly's identity is made of and
                                    the statement of what the code values mean)
  .media_id (BLAKE3)          ->   ExternalReference.metadata.memory_engine
                                     .media_id
  (resolved local path)       ->   ExternalReference.target_url, written as a
                                   file:// URL AT EXPORT TIME ONLY. The EDL
                                   itself stores no paths -- it is portable
                                   between machines precisely because it
                                   addresses content by hash. On import the
                                   hash in metadata wins over target_url.

 CONVENTIONS THAT KEEP THE ROUND TRIP EXACT

 - A plain cut is the ABSENCE of a Transition, matching OTIO, where adjacent
   clips simply butt together. Never emit a zero-length Transition for a cut.
 - Transitions sit between their two neighbours in the items list and overlap
   them by in_offset/out_offset. A TRANSITION DOES NOT CHANGE EITHER
   NEIGHBOUR'S TIMELINE EXTENT: the blend straddles the cut, covering the
   outgoing clip's last in_offset frames and the incoming clip's first
   out_offset frames, and the extra frames it needs beyond each clip's
   source_range are the HANDLES, drawn from available_range on either side.
   (This corrected an earlier statement here that the source_ranges already
   included the handles. They do not, in the golden fixture or in
   workers/render-video, and under that reading the fixture's timeline does
   not sum to the 899 frames its own validation report claims -- which is the
   arithmetic every beat lock in it depends on. See contracts#52.)
 - `timeline_range` on a Clip is derived (it is the running sum of preceding
   clip and gap EXTENTS -- see TimeEffect for what an extent is under a speed
   change -- and a transition does not subtract from it) and is NOT exported -- OTIO computes
   it. It is carried here only so a validator can catch a planner that emitted
   an inconsistent timeline, and it is excluded from the determinism digest.
 - Every RationalTime on a video track should share the timeline `rate`.
   Audio-track times may use the audio sample rate. OTIO permits mixed rates;
   this contract permits them only in that one place.

 See docs/otio-mapping.md for the exporter/importer pseudocode and the
 round-trip test plan.

edl_id.description: BLAKE3 over the canonical JSON of this EDL with the volatile fields removed. Two EDLs with the same id render identically.
edl_id.$comment:
THE ID MUST RECOMPUTE, OR IT IS NOT AN ID

 Canonical JSON is RFC 8785: keys sorted by UTF-16 code unit, no insignificant
 whitespace, numbers in ECMAScript Number::toString form (so 120.0 serialises
 as `120`), UTF-8 bytes. Exactly these five paths are removed before hashing,
 and no others:

   edl_id                          -- an id cannot cover itself
   determinism.generated_at        -- a wall clock would change the id per run
   validation.validated_at         -- ditto
   tracks[].items[].timeline_range -- derived, and excluded so re-deriving it
                                      never changes the id
   variant.sibling_edl_ids         -- each sibling's id would otherwise depend
                                      on every other sibling's

 The list is here rather than in one planner's docstring because the id is the
 render-cache key: a consumer that excludes a different set computes a
 different id for the same plan and silently misses the cache, or worse, hits
 it. contracts/tests recomputes it for every golden EDL -- an identity that is
 asserted rather than computed is how issue #26's invented span_id happened.

rate.description: Timeline rate in units per second. All video-track RationalTimes are expressed at this rate. Use exact NTSC rationals where the source demands it (30000/1001), never the rounded decimal.

global_start_time.description: Timeline zero, exported as OTIO Timeline.global_start_time. Normally 0; non-zero when the output must carry a broadcast start timecode such as 01:00:00:00.

media_refs.description: Every source this EDL touches, addressed by content hash. Declared once at the top so a renderer can resolve, verify and pre-open all sources before it starts, and so a missing source is a clean up-front failure rather than a crash at 80%.

tracks.description: Ordered tracks. Index 0 is the bottom video layer, matching OTIO Stack ordering.

reframe_tracks.description: Crop/reframe keyframe tracks, referenced by clips. Held at EDL level rather than inline on the clip so one subject-lock track can drive several clips from the same source shot.

color_pipeline.description: REQUIRED and non-null (contracts#58). It was nullable, and a null colour pipeline is a plan that declines to say what colour its own output is -- which leaves the renderer to decide, which is the whole defect. Every EDL states its colour path, including the ordinary all-SDR one, where the statement is short and the pipeline is an identity.

variant.description: Present when this EDL is one of several alternatives offered to the user. The reel planner emits 3-5; whichever the user picks becomes a PrefEvent, and the losers are training signal too.

RenderTarget.title: RenderTarget
RenderTarget.description: What this cut is for. Destination is part of the plan because the reframe, the loudness target and the duration are all chosen for it -- an Instagram cut is not a YouTube cut at a different bitrate.

encode.description: How the file is written. Required: `destination` says what the cut is FOR and settles nothing about the bytes, and a renderer that fills the difference in has made a delivery decision invisibly (contracts#56).

target_duration.description: What the planner was asked for. The realised duration is the sum of the timeline and may differ slightly, because landing a cut on a beat matters more than hitting exactly 30.000s.

max_duration.description: Hard ceiling imposed by the platform. Exceeding it is a validation failure, not a warning.

loudness_target_lufs.description: Integrated loudness the mix is normalised to. -14 for most social platforms, -23 for broadcast-style masters.

EncodeProfile.title: EncodeProfile
EncodeProfile.description: The delivery encode, stated in the plan rather than chosen by the renderer (contracts#56). Every field is mandatory somewhere in this object: there is no default profile, and no destination-to-codec table anywhere in a worker. Two plans that differ only in their encode are two different files, and `determinism.inputs_digest` covers this block for exactly that reason.
EncodeProfile.$comment:
WHY THIS IS CONTRACT DATA AND NOT WORKER CONFIGURATION

Before this existed, `workers/render-video` took the encode from a required
`JobSpec.params.encode` block, because RenderTarget said nothing about it. That
kept the renderer honest (it refused to guess) but left the plan unable to
describe its own output: two renders of one EDL could differ by an entire
codec and nothing recorded which was used. `Determinism.inputs_digest` claims
that two plans with the same digest are the same cut; that claim was false for
the one thing a viewer actually receives.

CODEC vs ENCODER, and why both are named.
`codec` is what a player has to understand. `encoder` is what produces the
bytes. They are not the same decision: libx264 and h264_videotoolbox both emit
H.264 and do not agree on a single byte, so a profile that named only the codec
would be reproducible in intent and not in fact. A renderer must refuse an
`encoder` that does not produce the declared `codec` -- that mismatch is a
planner error, not something to reconcile.

DETERMINISM.
`encoder_threads` is here for the same reason. It is not a performance knob in
this contract: x264 slices a frame across threads and the slice boundaries move
with the thread count, so an encode is only byte-reproducible on a machine that
used the same number. Stating it makes 'same EDL, same sources, same bytes' a
property of the plan rather than of the machine.

WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT HERE.
Container-level metadata (encoder version strings, creation time, chapters) is
not expressible and must not be written; a renderer strips it. Hardware-encoder
families are nameable via `encoder` but nothing here promises they are
reproducible across GPU driver versions -- a profile that wants byte-identical
output names a software encoder.

profile_id.description: Names this exact combination of settings, so a delivery preset is versioned contract data that review can see rather than a table inside a worker. Two profiles that differ in any field must not share an id.

container.description: The muxer. `mp4` and `mov` are delivery; `mkv` is what a lossless master goes in, because MP4 cannot carry FFV1.

scaler.description: Resampling kernel used to fit a crop to `resolution`. Pinned because the scaler touches every pixel of every frame, and two kernels are visibly different on a 480p proxy blown up to 1080p.

encoder_threads.description: Encoder thread count. A determinism input, not a performance setting -- see this def's $comment.

audio.description: Null only when the plan carries no audio at all. A program with audio and a null audio profile is a validation failure, not a silent mute.

encoder.description: Which implementation writes the bytes. Must produce `codec`; a renderer refuses the pair if it does not.

pixel_format.description: Chroma subsampling and bit depth in one value, which is how every encoder actually takes it.

preset.description: Encoder speed/efficiency preset, e.g. x264's `medium`. Null means the encoder's own default, which is only acceptable for encoders that have no preset axis (ffv1, prores_ks).

profile.description: Codec profile, e.g. `high` for H.264 or `main10` for HEVC. Null means the encoder derives it from pixel_format.

level.description: Codec level, e.g. `4.0`. Null means the encoder derives it from resolution and rate.

keyframe_interval_frames.description: Maximum GOP length in frames. Stated because it is a delivery decision with consequences a viewer feels -- a platform re-encoding a 10-second GOP seeks worse than one re-encoding a 2-second GOP -- and because leaving it to the encoder's default makes the same plan produce different files on different builds.

mode.description: `crf` and `cqp` take a quality value; `abr` and `cbr` take a bit rate; `lossless` takes neither.

quality.description: CRF or QP value. Required for crf and cqp, null otherwise.

bit_rate_kbps.description: Target bit rate. Required for abr and cbr, null otherwise.
Null for the lossless codecs, which have no bit rate to set.

MediaRef.title: MediaRef
MediaRef.description: One source, addressed by content hash rather than by path. This is what makes an EDL portable: the same plan renders on any machine that has the same footage, wherever it happens to live.

media_ref_id.description: Local alias used by clips within this EDL.

media_id.description: BLAKE3 of the source file, i.e. a MediaRecord primary key. For chaptered footage this is the span ASSEMBLY id; the renderer expands it to the ordered member files.

available_range.description: The full extent of the source, in source time. Exported as ExternalReference.available_range. A clip whose source_range escapes this is invalid and must fail validation before render, not during it.

is_span_assembly.description: True when media_id names a virtual assembly of chaptered files rather than a single file on disk.

member_media_ids.description: The assembly's members, in INDEX order -- the order they concatenate into one recording. Required when is_span_assembly is true and forbidden otherwise. This is the field that makes an assembly expandable from the EDL alone (contracts#55): the renderer never sees a MediaRecord, so before this existed the member order arrived out of band in the render job and the plan could not state what it had planned against.

continuity.description: Whether the chapters were verified gapless, copied from MediaRecord.Span.continuity. Required when is_span_assembly is true and forbidden otherwise.
continuity.$comment:
ONLY `verified_gapless` MAY BE RENDERED.

MediaRecord.Span already said why: 'Cameras occasionally drop a frame at the
split; the renderer must know before it concatenates.' A `verified_gap`
assembly concatenated as if it were gapless puts every source timecode after
the split wrong by the length of the gap, and every cut drawn from it lands on
the wrong frame -- silently, because the picture is still a picture.

So the contract, not the renderer, decides what happens: `verified_gap`,
`unverified` and `incomplete_set` are REFUSED at render. That is a structural
rule and not a judgement call -- there is no gap length in this contract to
compensate with, and inventing one is the failure this field exists to
prevent. A planner that wants such footage in a cut resolves it upstream: fill
the gap in ingest and re-verify, or plan against the individual members.

The renderer's own arithmetic check (summed member frame counts must equal
available_range.duration) stays as well. It catches the dropped frame that
nobody verified; this field catches the one that somebody verified and
recorded.

color_encoding.description: What this source's code values mean. REQUIRED for a video or image source and null for an audio or music one. Stated by the planner from the MediaRecord ingest already probed -- never inferred at render time, which is what `ColorPipeline.input_transform: "auto"` used to ask for (contracts#58).
color_encoding.$comment:
WHAT A RENDERER MAY DO WITH THIS, AND WHAT IT MUST NOT.

This field is the plan's ASSERTION about the source, and it wins. A renderer
must check it against whatever colour tags the container carries and REFUSE a
contradiction -- a plan that says bt709 over a file tagged bt2100_pq is either
the wrong file or a plan made before the file was re-graded, and both are
failures worth stopping for. An UNTAGGED source contradicts nothing, so the
declaration stands; that is the whole point of moving the decision to the
planner, where an untagged action-camera file is looked at once instead of
guessed at on every render.

source_peak_nits.description: Peak luminance this source is graded to, in cd/m^2. REQUIRED when `color_encoding` is an HDR member and null otherwise. For `bt2100_hlg` it MUST be 1000, because that is the nominal display the HLG decode is defined against here -- any other value would describe a decode that did not happen. It sits on the source rather than on ToneMap because a cut can hold a 1000-nit phone clip and a 4000-nit graded one.

label.description: Human-readable name for the NLE bin. Cosmetic only -- never used for resolution.

kind.description: Maps to OTIO Track.kind, which recognises exactly "Video" and "Audio".

role.description: What the track is for. Purely ours -- it rides in metadata -- but it lets the renderer build the filtergraph without inspecting contents.

items.description: Ordered children. Clips and gaps tile the track; transitions sit between two neighbours and overlap them.

source_range.description: In and out in SOURCE time, half-open. The single most important field in the contract: it is what the renderer seeks to, and it must round-trip through OTIO unchanged.

timeline_range.description: Derived position on the timeline. Carried for validation only; excluded from the determinism digest and not exported to OTIO, which recomputes it. Its DURATION is derived from source_range and any time_effect by the rule in TimeEffect's $comment -- equal to source_range.duration when there is no effect -- and its START is the running sum of the extents before it. A timeline_range that disagrees with that arithmetic is a validation failure, never a correction.

moment_id.description: The MomentRecord this clip realises. The provenance link that lets 'more of her' re-plan against the same candidate pool instead of starting over.

reframe_track_id.description: Reframe track driving this clip's crop. Null means full frame, letterboxed or pillarboxed per the target.

beat_lock.description: Present when this clip's in-point was snapped to the beat grid. Carries the alignment error so the <50ms quality gate is measurable from the plan alone, without rendering anything.

story_beat_id.description: Which story-arc beat this clip satisfies. Null on clips that are connective tissue rather than a required beat.

Gap.title: Gap
Gap.description: Explicit silence or black. Modelled explicitly, exactly as OTIO does, so a hold at the end of a film is a stated intention rather than an accident of arithmetic.

Transition.title: Transition
Transition.description: An overlap between the two neighbouring items. A hard cut is the absence of one of these, never a zero-length instance -- that is OTIO's convention and departing from it breaks the round trip.
Transition.$comment:
WHAT A TRANSITION IS, EXACTLY (contracts#52)

GEOMETRY. A transition does not change either neighbour's timeline extent. The
blend window straddles the cut: it covers the outgoing clip's last `in_offset`
frames and the incoming clip's first `out_offset` frames, and the frames it
needs beyond each clip's source_range are HANDLES drawn from available_range.
See the file-level $comment, which states the same thing for the OTIO mapping.

BLEND WEIGHT. Let L = in_offset + out_offset frames, and let output frame N run
0 <= N < L. The linear progress is u = N / L, and the weight applied to the
INCOMING picture is w = easing(u); the outgoing picture gets 1 - w. For a
dissolve that is out*(1-w) + in*w. For a dip, the first `in_offset` frames fade
the outgoing picture to the dip colour and the remaining `out_offset` frames
fade the incoming picture up from it, each using the same easing over its own
half.

EASING CURVES, written out because a name is not a curve. Each is a polynomial
in u over [0,1], using only + - and *, so every implementation lands on the
same bits -- the same reason ReframeKeyframe's `smooth` is a uniform rather
than a centripetal spline:

    linear       w = u
    ease_in      w = u*u*u
    ease_out     w = 1 - (1-u)*(1-u)*(1-u)
    ease_in_out  w = 4*u*u*u                     for u <  0.5
                 w = 1 - 4*(1-u)*(1-u)*(1-u)     for u >= 0.5

All four satisfy easing(0) = 0 and easing(1) = 1; ease_in_out is continuous at
u = 0.5, where both branches give 0.5.

AUDIO UNDER A TRANSITION. Nothing. The picture blends; the beds do not
cross-fade with it. Each clip's audio runs over that clip's own timeline extent
and stops at its out-point, so the sound butt-cuts at the cut frame while the
picture blends around it. This is a decision, and it is the same decision
contracts#59 made about music: a cross-fade is already expressible, exactly
once, as ClipAudio.fade_out on one clip and fade_in on the next, both of which
name their own curve. Letting a Transition ALSO imply an audio fade would put
two descriptions of one fade in one plan, and a renderer reading both applies
both.

TYPES. The enum holds only the transitions whose meaning is fixed by their
name and whose realisation is stated above. `wipe`, `push`, `blur_dissolve`,
`match_cut` and `custom` were removed along with the free-form `parameters`
object: none of them had an enumerated parameter set (a wipe needs at least an
angle, an edge softness and a direction), no planner emitted one, and a
transition type that no plan can describe and no renderer can execute is a
name, not a contract. A type enters this enum together with its parameters and
its stated realisation, or not at all. `match_cut` in particular is editorially
a HARD CUT, which is the absence of a Transition.

transition_type.description: `dissolve` maps to OTIO's standard SMPTE_Dissolve. The two dips map to OTIO "Custom" with the specific kind preserved in metadata, which is how OTIO itself handles non-standard transitions. See this def's $comment for why the enum is only three values.

in_offset.description: How far the transition extends backwards into the outgoing item.

out_offset.description: How far it extends forwards into the incoming item.

easing.description: Shape of the blend weight across the transition. Each value is a polynomial in the linear progress u, written out in this def's $comment; a name on its own is not a curve, and a cubic ease and a sine ease are different shots.

TimeEffect.title: TimeEffect
TimeEffect.description: Speed change. Restricted to what OTIO models natively, because a speed ramp that cannot round-trip is a speed ramp that silently disappears in Resolve. `source_range` stays authoritative under an effect and the timeline extent is derived from it -- see the $comment, which is the rule the renderer implements.
TimeEffect.$comment:
WHICH FIELD IS AUTHORITATIVE UNDER A TIME EFFECT (contracts#50)

 `Clip.source_range` is ALWAYS authoritative and ALWAYS means media: the
 frames actually read from the source, in the source's own time. It never
 changes meaning because an effect is attached to the clip.
 `Clip.timeline_range` is ALWAYS derived, and a validator recomputes it:

   no time_effect      timeline extent = source_range.duration
   linear_speed        timeline extent = source_range.duration / time_scalar
   freeze_frame        timeline extent = hold_duration

 and the clip's timeline START is, as ever, the running sum of the extents
 before it on the track (transitions do not change any extent -- see the
 top-of-file $comment).

 `time_scalar` keeps OTIO's LinearTimeWarp meaning exactly: it is the ratio
 of MEDIA time to TIMELINE time. 0.5 plays the media at half speed and so
 occupies twice as many timeline frames as it reads; 2.0 plays it at double
 speed and occupies half.

 WORKED EXAMPLE -- linear_speed, at rate 60000/1001

   source_range = { start_time 3062100, duration 56 }
   time_scalar  = 0.5
   => timeline extent = 56 / 0.5 = 112 frames
   The clip reads 56 frames of media and holds the timeline for 112.
   Output frame k of the clip (k = 0 .. 111) draws source frame
     source_range.start_time + floor(k * time_scalar)
   i.e. 3062100, 3062100, 3062101, 3062101, ... Each source frame is shown
   twice; nothing is interpolated, invented or blended. This sampling rule is
   part of the contract because otherwise one renderer duplicates frames and
   another synthesises them, and the two cuts are different footage.

   `time_scalar` must divide evenly: source_range.duration / time_scalar has
   to be a whole number of timeline frames. A plan that lands on a fractional
   frame is a validation failure, never a rounding -- rounding here is how a
   downbeat moves by half a frame per retimed clip.

 WORKED EXAMPLE -- freeze_frame, at rate 60000/1001

   source_range  = { start_time 3062100, duration 1 }
   freeze_at     = 3062100      (must equal source_range.start_time)
   hold_duration = 90
   => the clip reads exactly ONE frame and holds it for 90 timeline frames.
   source_range.duration must be exactly one frame at the timeline rate, so
   `source_range_within_available` still means what it says, and the hold's
   length is stated rather than inferred from a duration that is not one.

 WHY SOURCE AND NOT TIMELINE

 `source_range` is the field the renderer seeks to, and the one whose meaning
 has to survive a re-trim. Letting a speed change silently reinterpret it as
 a timeline extent would mean the same number denotes media on one clip and
 timeline on the next, with nothing in the file to say which -- and the
 failure mode is a cut landing exactly one retime factor late, which looks
 plausible in review.

 OTIO does not settle this: its own duration arithmetic ignores effects, so a
 naive importer that lays clips out by source_range.duration alone will place
 everything after a retimed clip early. That is a visible, immediate error
 rather than a subtle one, and docs/otio-mapping.md carries the export and
 import rule that avoids it.

 AUDIO UNDER A TIME EFFECT

 `audio_handling: mute` means the clip contributes NO ambient bed at all,
 whatever AmbientPlan gains would otherwise apply to it. `resample` plays the
 clip's audio at the same scalar (pitch moves with it); `preserve_pitch`
 time-stretches without moving pitch. Both non-mute modes are declarations a
 renderer may refuse until it can execute them bit-identically.

time_scalar.description: OTIO LinearTimeWarp.time_scalar: the ratio of media time to timeline time. 0.5 is half speed (twice the timeline extent), 2.0 is double. Required for linear_speed, and must divide source_range.duration into a whole number of timeline frames.

freeze_at.description: Source time to hold. Required for freeze_frame, and must equal source_range.start_time -- the frozen frame is the one frame the clip reads.

hold_duration.description: How long the frozen frame is held, in TIMELINE time. Required for freeze_frame, forbidden otherwise: it is the clip's timeline extent, and without it a freeze has a start and no end.

audio_handling.description: What happens to this clip's audio under a speed change. Almost always `mute` for slow motion, because pitch-shifted ambient sounds broken. `mute` suppresses this clip's ambient bed entirely, whatever AmbientPlan says about it.

ColorOp.title: ColorOp
ColorOp.description: A per-clip colour adjustment, planned by the intelligence layer and merely applied by the renderer. `amount` is normalised to [-1,1]; what that means in light is stated in this def's $comment, per op, as a formula (contracts#49).
ColorOp.$comment:
THE TRANSFER FUNCTION FROM `amount` TO A PICTURE (contracts#49)

Before this, `amount` was 'signed, normalised to [-1,1] where 0 is no change',
which pins the sign and the zero and nothing else. `{"op":"exposure",
"amount":0.12}` could mean +0.12 stops, +1.2 stops, a 12% linear gain or a 12%
move towards a clipping ceiling. Two renderers that both follow the contract
produce visibly different pictures, and neither looks wrong in review. Colour
is the one thing where a silent disagreement survives all the way to print.

WHERE THE OPS APPLY.
In `color_pipeline.working_space`, which is LINEAR-LIGHT RGB scaled so that 1.0
is reference white. Not in the source's encoding and not in the output's: an
exposure adjustment is a multiplication of light, and a multiplication applied
to a gamma-encoded code value is not one. Values are NOT clamped between ops --
a saturation of -1 followed by an exposure is well defined -- and are clamped
to [0,1] exactly once, when the pipeline encodes to `output_encoding`.

THE TABLE. `a` is `amount`. R, G, B are linear working-space channels.

  op          physical quantity        formula
  ----------  -----------------------  --------------------------------------
  exposure    +/- 2 stops              RGB' = RGB * 2^(2a)
  saturation  0x .. 2x chroma          Y    = kr*R + kg*G + kb*B
                                       RGB' = Y + (1 + a) * (RGB - Y)

  (kr, kg, kb) are the working space's own luminance coefficients:
    linear_bt709   0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722   (ITU-R BT.709-6 Table 3)
    linear_bt2020  0.2627, 0.6780, 0.0593   (ITU-R BT.2020-2 Table 4)
  They are named rather than assumed because using BT.709's vector on BT.2020
  primaries desaturates greens by several percent, which reads as 'the grade'.

  a = 0 is the identity in both rows: 2^0 = 1, and 1 + 0 = 1.

COMPOSITION.
Ops apply in array order, left to right. Both ops are LINEAR maps of the RGB
vector, so the whole list composes into one 3x3 matrix; a renderer MUST form
that matrix by multiplying the per-op matrices in array order in IEEE-754
binary64 and apply it once, rather than applying each op in turn. That is not
an optimisation, it is what makes the result reproducible: applying them one at
a time rounds at every step, and the rounding depends on how many ops the
planner happened to emit. The chain runs at no less than binary32 per channel.

WHY THIS ENUM IS SHORT, AND WHAT LEFT.
Every value removed here was removed because `amount: number` cannot carry what
the op needs, not because the look is unwanted. Each has a follow-up issue so
the capability is lost out loud rather than quietly:

  match_to_reference, auto_white_balance -- both require the renderer to MEASURE
    an image and derive a grade from it. That is an intelligence-layer
    computation, it is not reproducible across builds, and hard rule 3 puts it
    on the planner's side. The planner resolves them into the primitive ops it
    wants applied. `reference_clip_id` survives as pure provenance.
  temperature, tint -- a colour temperature is a chromatic adaptation BETWEEN
    two illuminants, and this contract states only one white point. '+2000 K'
    from what? A relative mired shift is statable, but it also needs a named
    adaptation matrix (Bradford and CAT02 disagree), and an unnamed one is
    exactly the invisible-until-print choice this issue is about. A
    `white_balance` op carrying source and target white points as CIE xy plus a
    named adaptation matrix is the right shape.
  highlights, shadows -- need a tonal mask: a pivot and a rolloff width. One
    scalar cannot carry a selection.
  lift, gamma, gain -- these are the ASC CDL's offset, power and slope, and the
    CDL defines them PER CHANNEL. Collapsed to one scalar, `gain` is `exposure`
    under another name and `lift` and `gamma` are a grade nobody can match a
    shot with. The right shape is an ASC CDL op (ANSI/SMPTE S-2016-001) with
    slope/offset/power triples, which needs no invention at all.
  contrast -- a power about a pivot is not a linear map, so it cannot fuse into
    the matrix above; it needs its own value space and its own statement about
    where clipping happens.
  lut -- a LUT is an ASSET, not an amount. It needs a content hash so the plan
    addresses it the way it addresses everything else, a cube size, a domain,
    and an interpolation rule (trilinear and tetrahedral differ on exactly the
    skin tones a family album is made of). `lut_id` was a slug pointing at
    nothing resolvable and is removed with the op.

op.description: Which adjustment. The enum is short on purpose -- see the $comment for what was removed and why, and for the issue that carries each removed capability.

amount.description: Signed, normalised to [-1,1] where 0 is no change. Exposure: a * 2 stops. Saturation: a chroma scale of 1 + a. A single normalised scale keeps ops composable and makes 'is this grade aggressive' a question with an answer.

reference_clip_id.description: PROVENANCE ONLY -- a renderer never reads this field. The clip whose look this adjustment was derived from, recorded so a shot-matching decision stays auditable in the plan after the planner has resolved it into primitive ops. It resolves nothing at render time: the ops beside it are the whole instruction.

ClipAudio.title: ClipAudio
ClipAudio.description: This clip's own sound, and the ONLY place its level is stated (contracts#53).
ClipAudio.$comment:
THE GAIN IS STATED ONCE, HERE.

AmbientPlan used to carry `default_gain_db` and a `per_clip_gain_db` override
list alongside this field, so a clip's bed had two levels and the contract had
no composition rule. In the golden fixture that was 14 dB of ambiguity: every
clip carried gain_db -14 while the ambient plan said -14 with two per-clip
overrides, and summing, overriding and ignoring were all defensible readings of
the same plan. `workers/render-video` refused the combination rather than pick.

The fix is the one contracts#59 applied to music: state it once. A clip's
ambient level is `gain_db` on that clip, in dB relative to the source, and
nothing else adjusts it. The planner's own notion of a default level is a
planner setting -- it decides what to write here and does not travel with the
plan.

The field is REQUIRED, with no default: a level a renderer has to supply is a
level nobody chose.

gain_db.description: Level of this clip's own audio, in dB relative to the source. Composes with nothing else in the plan except MixPlan.master_gain_db and any DuckingRule whose target role covers this clip's track.

fade_in.description: Fade length at the clip's in-point. The curve is a LINEAR RAMP IN AMPLITUDE from 0 to 1 over the declared frames -- not equal-power, not linear in dB (contracts#60). Equal-power is the usual choice for a music crossfade and would be audibly different on a long fade, so it is named here rather than left to the mixer; a planner that wants a different shape emits a Transition.

fade_out.description: Fade length ending on the clip's last frame, a linear ramp in amplitude from 1 to 0. Same convention as fade_in.

audio_extends_past_out.description: L-cut: hold this clip's audio past its visual out-point, so a laugh finishes over the next shot. Realises MomentRecord.safe_trim.preserve_audio_tail.

BeatLock.title: BeatLock
BeatLock.description: Records that a cut was placed against the music rather than merely near it. `alignment_error_ms` is the audit trail for the <50ms downbeat quality gate.

alignment_error_ms.description: Signed distance from the clip's timeline in-point to the beat. Negative is early. Non-zero because a cut must also land on a certified snap point, and the nearest snap point is rarely exactly on the beat -- the planner trades a few milliseconds of beat error for a cut that lands on a real motion onset.

snap_point_kind.description: Which MomentRecord snap point the cut actually landed on.

Marker.title: Marker
Marker.description: Maps to otio.schema.Marker. Markers are how our reasoning becomes visible to a human editor who opens the timeline in Resolve.

ReframeTrack.title: ReframeTrack
ReframeTrack.description: A crop keyframe track that turns landscape footage into a vertical cut with the subject held in frame. This is core IP and has no OTIO equivalent, so it round-trips through metadata.

keyframes.description: Ordered by time, at least one. A single keyframe is a static crop; the interesting case is a moving crop that tracks a subject across the frame.

fallback.description: What to do if subject tracking fails at render time. Never leave this implicit: a reframe that silently falls back to a centre crop can decapitate the subject of the shot.

time.description: SOURCE time of the keyframe, so the track stays valid if the clip is later trimmed or retimed.

crop.description: Crop window in normalised source coordinates. Its aspect must match the track's target_aspect_ratio; a mismatch is a validation failure because the renderer must not be the one deciding how to reconcile it.

interpolation.description: How to reach the NEXT keyframe. `hold` produces a snap, which is occasionally what a hard beat wants. Every mode is a stated formula, not a name -- see the $comment.
interpolation.$comment:
INTERPOLATION IS A FORMULA, NOT AN ADJECTIVE (contracts#51)

 Let the keyframes of a track be K[0..n-1] with strictly increasing source
 times t[0..n-1] and crop values P[0..n-1]. Each component of the crop box
 (x, y, w, h) is interpolated INDEPENDENTLY and identically. For a source
 frame f with t[i] <= f < t[i+1], let

   u = (f - t[i]) / (t[i+1] - t[i])          -- so u is in [0, 1)

 and let the mode be the one declared on K[i] (the keyframe being left, not
 the one being reached).

   linear  value = P[i] + (P[i+1] - P[i]) * u

   hold    value = P[i]   for every f in the interval. The snap happens at
           t[i+1], where the next interval takes over.

   bezier  A cubic Bezier easing with P0=(0,0) and P3=(1,1) and the two
           `bezier_control` points as P1 and P2, in (time, value) normalised
           keyframe-interval space -- CSS's cubic-bezier(). Solve x(s) = u for
           s, then value = P[i] + (P[i+1] - P[i]) * y(s).

   smooth  A UNIFORM Catmull-Rom spline through the keyframe values, endpoints
           clamped. With

             A = P[i-1], clamped to P[i]   when i == 0
             B = P[i]
             C = P[i+1]
             D = P[i+2], clamped to P[i+1] when i+2 > n-1

           value = 0.5 * ( (2*B)
                         + (-A + C) * u
                         + (2*A - 5*B + 4*C - D) * u^2
                         + (-A + 3*B - 3*C + D) * u^3 )

 WHY THIS CURVE, AND WHY UNIFORM

 `smooth` is what a subject-tracking crop wants: it is C1 at every interior
 keyframe, so the crop has no visible velocity step where one keyframe hands
 over to the next, and it passes exactly through every keyframe, so the
 positions the planner stated are the positions rendered.

 CLAMPING THE ENDPOINTS IS AN EASE, NOT A STRAIGHT LINE. The tangent at K[i]
 is (P[i+1] - P[i-1]) / 2; with P[-1] clamped to P[0] that is half the first
 segment's slope, so the crop eases into the track and out of it rather than
 starting at full speed. On a TWO-keyframe track the whole path is that ease:

   value = B + (C - B) * (0.5*u + 1.5*u^2 - u^3)

 which passes through both keyframes, is monotone (its derivative,
 0.5 + 3u - 3u^2, has a minimum of 0.5 on [0,1]), never leaves [B, C], and
 reaches the midpoint at u = 0.5. It is NOT a lerp -- a planner that wants a
 constant-velocity pan asks for `linear`.

 UNIFORM means the tangents are built from neighbouring VALUES only; the
 spacing of t[] does not enter the formula. The centripetal variant is better
 behaved on unevenly spaced keyframes, and it is rejected here for one
 reason: it needs a fourth root of a distance, and pow() is not bit-identical
 across platforms and libms. The uniform form uses only +, - and *, so every
 conforming implementation lands on the same IEEE-754 double, which is what
 `edl_id` promises. A planner that wants spacing-aware easing has `bezier`,
 whose curve it states explicitly.

 Catmull-Rom overshoots: between two keyframes the value can leave the
 interval [P[i], P[i+1]]. That is the point (it is what makes the motion look
 like a camera move rather than a series of ramps) and it is the PLANNER's
 job to keep the interpolated path inside the frame. A renderer that finds a
 crop leaving the source frame fails; it does not clamp, because a clamp is
 how a crop silently slides off its subject.

 Interpolation is evaluated against integer SOURCE frame numbers, never
 against seconds, so a retimed clip (see TimeEffect) samples the same curve
 at the source frames it actually reads.

bezier_control.description: Control points for bezier interpolation, as (x,y) in normalised keyframe-interval space.

confidence.description: Tracker confidence at this keyframe. Low-confidence stretches are where the fallback earns its keep.

subject_ref.description: The tracked entity: a SAM 2 object id, a face track uuid, or null for saliency.

keep_in_frame.description: The part of the subject that must never leave the crop. `head` is the one that matters for people: a technically-centred crop that clips a forehead reads as a mistake.

headroom.description: Fraction of the crop height kept above the subject's head. Composition rule, planned rather than hard-coded in the renderer.

ReframeSmoothing.title: ReframeSmoothing
ReframeSmoothing.description: Constraints that stop a reframe from looking like a nervous camera operator. Raw per-frame subject centroids are far too jittery to use directly.

max_velocity_per_second.description: Cap on crop travel, in normalised units per second. The difference between a considered pan and a whip.

deadzone.description: Subject movement smaller than this does not move the crop at all, which is what keeps a mostly-still subject from causing constant micro-drift.

AudioPlan.title: AudioPlan
AudioPlan.description: The complete audio intention: what music plays, how much of the original scene survives under it, and how the two are balanced against each other over time.

ducking.description: Ordered ducking rules. Later rules win where they overlap, which keeps the resolution deterministic instead of depending on the renderer's mixer implementation; DuckingRule's $comment states exactly what 'overlap' means once the rules have attack and release ramps.

MusicCue.title: MusicCue
MusicCue.description: Licence and provenance for one piece of music, attached to the clips that place it. A cue is NOT a placement: the bed lives on an audio track like every other sound, and the cue says what it is and what may legally be done with it.
MusicCue.$comment:
MUSIC IS PLACED ONCE (contracts#59)

 This type used to carry `source_range`, `timeline_range`, `gain_db`,
 `fade_in` and `fade_out` as well as a licence, which meant a well-formed EDL
 described the same bed twice: once as an audio-track Clip and once here. A
 renderer that summed them played the music 6 dB hot; a renderer that read
 one of them was guessing which. Both are plausible and neither is loud.

 The track placement is authoritative, for three reasons: it is the
 OTIO-native structure (a Clip on a Track with kind "Audio"), it is what
 survives a round trip into Resolve, and `Track.role` already tells the mixer
 which bed is music without inspecting its contents. So the cue keeps only
 what a placement cannot express -- the licence -- plus `clip_ids`, which
 says which placements it covers.

 LOOPING (contracts#57)

 There is deliberately no `loop` flag. A bed that has to cover more timeline
 than the track offers is emitted as SEVERAL clips, one per pass, each with
 its own source_range and timeline_range and each listed in `clip_ids`. The
 loop join is then an ordinary cut between two ordinary clips: its restart
 point is visible in the plan, its truncation is visible in the plan, and a
 crossfade across the join -- if the planner wants one -- is an ordinary
 Transition. A boolean could express none of that, and every unstated part of
 it (butt or crossfade, restart at the cue's in-point or the track's start,
 truncate or overrun) moves the bed against the BeatGrid, which is the one
 thing every beat-locked cut in the timeline depends on.

 `BeatGrid.source_cue_id` still names a cue, and the grid is still authored
 in timeline time, so the anchor resolves exactly as before.

media_ref_id.description: The source this cue licenses. Must equal the media_ref_id of every clip in clip_ids.

clip_ids.description: The audio-track clips that place this cue, in timeline order. One entry for a bed that plays once, one per pass for a bed that repeats. Every clip on a track whose role is `music` must be claimed by exactly one cue -- that is how an unlicensed bed becomes impossible rather than merely unlikely.

license.description: Required, not optional. Music licensing is a Phase 0 decision precisely because an unlicensed track in a shared reel is a legal problem, and the plan is the place it becomes checkable.

cleared_for.description: Where this cut may legally be published. `user_supplied` music is typically personal_use only, and a share flow must be able to refuse rather than discover the problem after upload.

AmbientPlan.title: AmbientPlan
AmbientPlan.description: Processing applied to the location sound as a whole. Keeping real ambient under music is most of what separates a film that feels like a memory from a slideshow with a soundtrack -- but the LEVEL of each clip's bed lives on that clip (ClipAudio.gain_db), and this type carries only what is a property of the group rather than of one clip.
AmbientPlan.$comment:
WHAT THIS TYPE LOST, AND WHY (contracts#53)

This def used to hold five more fields. Each is gone for a stated reason, and
none of them is coming back in the same shape:

  `default_gain_db` and `per_clip_gain_db` -- a second place to state a level
  that ClipAudio.gain_db already states. See ClipAudio's $comment.

  `enabled` -- a second way to say a bed is silent. `ClipAudio.muted` already
  says it, per clip, where a reader can see which sound is gone. A plan with a
  global switch and a per-clip switch has to define which wins.

  `preserve_speech` -- not executable by a renderer at all: nothing in an EDL
  says which clips contain speech (that lives in MomentRecord.transcript,
  which the renderer never sees) and detecting it at mix time is both a
  creative decision and not reproducible. It described a PLANNER rule, and the
  planner already realises it in the plan, as a raised ClipAudio.gain_db on
  the speech clips plus a DuckingRule over the ranges those clips occupy.

  `noise_suppression: none | light | moderate | aggressive` -- a strength
  label with no algorithm, no parameters and no measurable target behind it.
  'Moderate' is a slider caption; two implementations differ audibly and
  neither is wrong. It is not re-specified here because a denoiser is not a
  mix decision at all: if a bed needs cleaning, `workers/enhance` produces a
  cleaned rendition, that rendition is a MediaRecord with its own content
  hash, and the plan points at it. That keeps the renderer dumb and keeps the
  processing auditable and cacheable, which a flag on a mix could not.

What is left is a linear filter with a stated response, which a renderer can
execute and any two implementations agree on.

high_pass.description: Removes wind rumble, which otherwise dominates every outdoor action clip. Null means no filter. Applied ONCE to the summed ambient group -- after each clip's gain, fades and L-cut tail, before any DuckingRule -- so that the plan's order of operations is stated rather than left to a mixer's internal graph.
high_pass.$comment:
THE CORNER WAS PINNED AND THE FILTER WAS NOT (contracts#53)

The old field was `high_pass_hz`, a bare frequency. A 2-pole Butterworth and a
4-pole Linkwitz-Riley at 120 Hz remove different amounts of exactly the thing
the field exists to remove, so a corner alone does not describe a filter.

The response is BUTTERWORTH (maximally flat passband), realised as a cascade
of RBJ-cookbook high-pass biquads at the same corner frequency, one biquad per
two poles, with the standard Butterworth Q values:

    order 2   one section,  Q = 0.70710678118654752
    order 4   two sections, Q = 0.54119610014619698 then Q = 1.30656296487637652

The corner is the -3 dB point of the whole cascade for order 2; for order 4 the
Q pair is the standard factorisation, which puts the cascade's -3 dB point at
the same corner. Order is restricted to 2 and 4 because those are the two the
cascade above defines; an odd order needs a first-order section and a different
rule, and nothing has asked for one.

This is a specification by PROCESS rather than by outcome, which this contract
usually avoids -- but a linear filter is the case where process is exact:
given the corner, the order and the Q values, the coefficients are determined
and every implementation lands on the same numbers. A target ('at most -18 dB
at 60 Hz') would have left the passband ripple free.

order.description: Pole count. See AmbientPlan.high_pass's $comment for the Q values each order expands to.

DuckingRule.title: DuckingRule
DuckingRule.description: One duck: turn `target` down by `reduction_db` over these timeline ranges, on the envelope this def's $comment states exactly.
DuckingRule.$comment:
THE ENVELOPE, WRITTEN OUT (contracts#54)

A reduction, a range and two time constants do not describe a gain curve, and
the difference between the plausible readings is several dB in the middle of
the ramp -- which is exactly where the voice the duck exists for is sitting.
So:

GAIN MOVES LINEARLY IN dB. Not linearly in amplitude, and not on the
exponential one-pole curve a hardware compressor would use. Linear in dB is
the reading a person gets from writing '9 dB over 80 ms' and it is the only one
that is exactly reproducible without naming a filter.

THE ATTACK RAMP ENDS AT THE RANGE START; THE RELEASE RAMP BEGINS AT THE RANGE
END. So the declared range is fully ducked for its whole declared extent, and
the ramps sit outside it. For one range [s, e) in timeline seconds, with
a = attack_ms/1000 and r = release_ms/1000, the reduction in dB at time t is:

    t <  s - a            0
    s - a <= t < s        reduction_db * (t - (s - a)) / a
    s <= t <  e           reduction_db
    e <= t <  e + r       reduction_db * (1 - (t - e) / r)
    t >= e + r            0

with a = 0 and r = 0 degenerating to a step, which is what
`workers/render-video` implemented while this was unspecified. A ramp that
reaches before frame 0 or past the end of the timeline is simply not rendered
there; the envelope is a function of timeline time and the timeline is what it
is.

WITHIN ONE RULE the envelope is the MAXIMUM over that rule's own ranges, which
is what makes two ranges closer together than attack + release well defined
rather than a race between a release and the next attack.

ACROSS RULES the existing resolution still holds -- later rules win where they
overlap -- now stated precisely: a rule's SUPPORT is its ranges each extended
by a before and r after. At any instant t, the reduction applied to a target is
the envelope of the highest-indexed rule whose support contains t; every other
rule contributes nothing at t. That keeps 'duck everything, except here' 
expressible (a later rule may reduce by 0 dB), which a maximum could not.

WHAT LEFT THIS TYPE

`trigger` is gone. Its non-`explicit_ranges` values (`speech`, `music`,
`ambient`) asked the renderer to analyse the mix at render time, which is both
a decision and not reproducible across builds; the schema already called
explicit ranges 'always preferred, because it is deterministic'. Detection is
planner-side, and the planner resolves it to ranges before it emits an EDL.
With the other three gone the field held one value, so it holds none.

`threshold_db` and `ratio` are gone with it: they are compressor parameters,
they were nullable and null in every plan ever emitted, and there is no
compressor here to hang them on.

`ranges` is now required and non-empty. A duck with no extent is an intent, not
a plan.

target.description: Which Track.role gets turned down. A rule whose target matches no track in the plan states an intent about audio that does not exist, and is a validation failure.

reduction_db.description: Positive number of dB to reduce by, reached at the range start and held to the range end.

attack_ms.description: Length of the ramp DOWN, ending at the range start. 0 is a step.

release_ms.description: Length of the ramp back UP, beginning at the range end. 0 is a step.

ranges.description: Timeline ranges held at the full reduction. Non-empty, and each must lie within the timeline.

BeatGrid.title: BeatGrid
BeatGrid.description: The musical skeleton the cut is hung on. Stored as explicit per-beat times rather than as a BPM to be extrapolated, because real tracks drift and an extrapolated grid is 200ms out by the end of a 30-second reel.

beats.description: Every beat, in TIMELINE time, ordered. Downbeats are flagged rather than stored separately so a cut can reference one index regardless of which it turned out to be.

analyzer.description: Which beat tracker produced this. Recorded partly for reproducibility and partly because the licence-safe analyser (librosa, ISC) and the more accurate but non-commercial ones (madmom) must never be confused.

tolerance_ms.description: Maximum acceptable beat-alignment error for a cut claiming to be beat-locked. The quality gate is 50ms on downbeats.

section.description: Musical section this beat falls in. Lets the planner put the visual peak on the drop rather than merely on a loud beat.

StoryArc.title: StoryArc
StoryArc.description: The narrative intention, kept with the plan so that a revision instruction such as 'more of her' or 'less drone' re-satisfies the SAME arc instead of re-planning from scratch. That persistence is what makes iterative editing feel like direction rather than dice-rolling.

logline.description: One sentence the arc is trying to say. Written by the frontier model and shown to the user, so a plan can be judged before it is rendered.

energy_curve.description: Target energy over the timeline, as sampled control points. The planner satisfies it mechanically by choosing moments whose features match; it is a specification, not a description.

source.description: Who authored the arc. A tier3_model arc must carry its ConsentRef, because producing it meant sending a contact sheet off the device.

prompt_id.description: Which prompt-engine template produced it, so a prompt regression is traceable to the outputs it affected.

rationale.description: The model's stated reasoning, kept for the user-facing 'why this cut' explanation and for eval review.

intent.description: What this act is for, in plain language: 'arrival, establish where we are'.

StoryBeat.title: StoryBeat
StoryBeat.description: A required narrative element and the clips that satisfy it. An unsatisfied required beat is a validation failure -- that is the mechanism by which 'the film has an arc' is checked rather than hoped for.

candidate_moment_ids.description: Moments the planner considered for this beat. Retained so a revision can swap in an alternative without re-running retrieval.

ColorEncoding.title: ColorEncoding
ColorEncoding.description: What a set of code values MEANS: primaries, transfer function and matrix coefficients, as one token. The spelling is closed -- see this def's $comment for the table each token expands to.
ColorEncoding.$comment:
THE VALUE SPACE, ENUMERATED (contracts#58)

`input_transform` and `output_transform` used to be bare strings, so "rec709",
"bt709" and "Rec. 709" were all equally valid contract data and none of them
named a primaries set. A colour encoding is three facts, not one, and all three
change the picture:

  token         primaries                    transfer                  matrix
  ------------  ---------------------------  ------------------------  ---------
  srgb          BT.709 (D65)                 IEC 61966-2-1             BT.709
  bt709         BT.709 (D65)                 ITU-R BT.709-6 OETF       BT.709
  display_p3    SMPTE RP 431-2 (D65)         IEC 61966-2-1             BT.709
  bt2020_sdr    ITU-R BT.2020-2 (D65)        ITU-R BT.709-6 OETF       BT.2020 non-constant
  bt2100_pq     ITU-R BT.2020-2 (D65)        SMPTE ST 2084 (PQ)        BT.2020 non-constant
  bt2100_hlg    ITU-R BT.2020-2 (D65)        ARIB STD-B67 (HLG)        BT.2020 non-constant

`srgb` and `bt709` share primaries and differ ONLY in the transfer: sRGB's
piecewise curve is roughly gamma 2.2 and BT.709's OETF is roughly gamma 1/0.45
with a different toe. They are listed separately because that difference is
about two code values in the shadows of every frame, which is where banding
lives.

HDR MEMBERS AND WHAT THEY DECODE TO.
  bt2100_pq  -- ST 2084 is ABSOLUTE: a code value names a luminance in cd/m^2
                directly, so the decode needs no assumption at all.
  bt2100_hlg -- HLG is relative, and its EOTF is the inverse OETF followed by
                the OOTF, whose system gamma depends on the peak luminance of
                the display being modelled. This contract fixes that at the
                BT.2100 nominal: PEAK 1000 cd/m^2, SYSTEM GAMMA 1.2, so HLG
                reference white (signal 0.75) decodes to 203 cd/m^2. Stated
                because leaving it open is what makes one HLG render look flat
                and another look right, and `MediaRef.source_peak_nits`
                is required to be 1000 for an HLG source for the same reason.

EVERY TOKEN IS LIMITED RANGE ("video range", ffprobe's `tv`), for the source and
for the delivered file alike. Range is part of what a code value MEANS, so it
belongs in this table rather than in a renderer's habits: reading full-range
levels as limited crushes the blacks and clips the whites, reading limited as
full washes the picture out, and neither raises anything. A full-range source
is therefore refused rather than guessed at. Phones do shoot full range, so a
full-range variant of each token is a real gap, filed as contracts#101 -- it is
left out here because adding a token nobody can round-trip is worse than
refusing.

DELIVERY IS SDR AT v0. `ColorPipeline.output_encoding` accepts only the four
SDR members. HDR delivery needs a mastering-display block (MaxCLL, MaxFALL,
mastering primaries) that no worker writes today, and shipping the enum without
it would let a plan ask for a file the renderer cannot label correctly.

ToneMap.title: ToneMap
ToneMap.description: How HDR light is fitted into the SDR output volume. Required exactly when some source carries an HDR encoding; null otherwise, because a tone map over SDR sources is a grade nobody asked for.
ToneMap.$comment:
THE OPERATOR IS NAMED AND ITS CURVE IS WRITTEN OUT (contracts#58)

`tone_map_hdr_to_sdr` was a boolean, correctly justified -- left implicit, HDR
sources render washed out -- that named no operator. Hable, Mobius and Reinhard
differ substantially on exactly the material that triggers them, a bright sky
behind a backlit face, and the peak-luminance assumption moves the result
again. So the one field that existed to stop HDR rendering wrong did not
determine what it rendered as.

NORMALISATION, FIRST, BECAUSE EVERY NUMBER BELOW DEPENDS ON IT.
The working space is linear light scaled so that 1.0 is `reference_white_nits`.
Every source is linearised into that scale before anything else happens, so a
PQ source graded to 1000 cd/m^2 with `reference_white_nits: 100` arrives with
its peak at 10.0. Define

    peak = MediaRef.source_peak_nits / reference_white_nits     (peak >= 1)

AN SDR SOURCE HAS NO PEAK FIELD BECAUSE IT NEEDS NONE. `reference_white_nits`
IS what an SDR code value of 1.0 means, so an SDR source always linearises with
its diffuse white at exactly 1.0 whatever the number is set to. Setting it to
203 therefore does not brighten the SDR footage; it asserts that this
programme's diffuse white is 203 cd/m^2, which is where an HDR source's 203-nit
level then lands too. That alignment is the only thing the field does, and it
is why it is one number for the whole plan rather than one per source.

IT APPLIES TO HDR SOURCES ONLY. A cut may hold an HDR clip and an SDR one; the
tone map runs on the HDR ones and the SDR ones pass through untouched. This is
not a nicety: an SDR source has no `source_peak_nits`, so its `peak` would be 1,
and every operator at peak 1 is a compression curve rather than the identity --
hable at peak 1 darkens mid-grey by about a third. Matching an HDR clip and an
SDR clip across a cut is a PLANNER decision, expressed as `color_ops` on one of
them, not something the tone map does by accident.

PEAK IS PER SOURCE, NOT PER PLAN. It lives on the MediaRef beside the encoding
it belongs to, because a cut can hold a 1000-nit phone clip and a 4000-nit
graded one, and fitting both from one number maps one of them wrong. Everything
else here -- the operator, its parameter, the reference white, the desaturation
threshold -- is a look, and a look is one decision for the whole programme.

WHAT THE OPERATOR DOES.
Per pixel, on linear working-space RGB, in this order:

  1. DESATURATION, before mapping. With luminance coefficients (kr,kg,kb) from
     the working space (the same vector ColorOp.saturation uses):

         Y  = kr*R + kg*G + kb*B
         ob = max(Y - desaturation, eps) / max(Y, eps)          eps = 1e-6
         RGB <- RGB * (1 - ob) + Y * ob

     `desaturation` is therefore a THRESHOLD in units of reference white, not a
     strength: a pixel dimmer than it is untouched, and a pixel brighter than
     it is pulled towards its own luminance in proportion to how far past it
     is. `desaturation: 0` disables it (ob collapses to eps/Y). This is what
     stops a 4000-nit sun turning into a flat cyan disc when its brightest
     channel is compressed and the others are not.

  2. MAPPING, on the brightest channel, applied to all three as one scale, so
     hue is preserved by construction:

         s     = max(R, G, B, eps)
         RGB' = RGB * f(s) / s

  3. f is the named operator. All three satisfy f(peak) = 1, so the source
     peak lands exactly on output reference white and nothing above it exists:

     hable     f(s) = H(s) / H(peak),  where H is the Uncharted-2 curve
                 H(x) = (x*(A*x + C*B) + D*E) / (x*(A*x + B) + D*F) - E/F
                 A=0.15  B=0.50  C=0.10  D=0.20  E=0.02  F=0.30
               Takes no parameter, so `operator_param` must be null.
     reinhard  offset = (1 - operator_param) / operator_param
                 f(s) = s / (s + offset) * (peak + offset) / peak
               `operator_param` is in (0,1), OPEN AT BOTH ENDS. As it
               approaches 0 the offset grows without bound and f approaches a
               straight scale by 1/peak; at exactly 1 the offset is 0 and f
               collapses to the CONSTANT 1.0 -- every pixel above black
               becomes reference white, which is a white frame, not a grade.
               The first draft of this table said 1 was the straight scale.
               It is the other end. Measuring the filter is what caught it.
     mobius    j = operator_param
                 f(s) = s                                        for s <= j
                 a    = -j*j*(peak - 1) / (j*j - 2*j + peak)
                 b    = (j*j - 2*j*peak + peak) / max(peak - 1, 1e-6)
                 f(s) = (b*b + 2*b*j + j*j) / (b - a) * (s + a) / (s + b)
               Linear below j and compressive above it, so highlights roll off
               and everything under j is untouched.

These formulas are NORMATIVE. They were derived by measuring a renderer rather
than copied from one, and workers/render-video carries a test that feeds known
linear values through the real filter and checks the output against them --
because a formula in a schema that no implementation matches is worse than the
gap it replaced.

WHAT IS NOT HERE. No target peak: every operator maps each source's `peak` to
1.0, which IS the target, and a second number that must equal reference white
is a second place to be wrong. No BT.2390 EETF: it is the better operator, and no
renderer in this repo can execute it. A specification neither side can satisfy
is worse than the gap it was meant to close.

operator.description: Which curve. Formulas are written out in this def's $comment and are normative.

operator_param.description: The operator's single shape parameter: reinhard's contrast, mobius's linear-section end. Null for hable, which has none. There is no default -- a curve parameter a renderer supplies is a curve nobody chose. The range is OPEN AT BOTH ENDS for both parameterised operators, and 1 is excluded because it is degenerate rather than merely extreme: see the $comment.

reference_white_nits.description: What 1.0 means in the working space, in cd/m^2. 100 is SDR diffuse white (BT.1886); 203 is the BT.2100 HLG graphic-white convention. Required because it is the scale every other number in this object is expressed against.

desaturation.description: Threshold, in units of reference white, above which a pixel is pulled towards its own luminance before mapping. 0 disables it. See the $comment for the exact formula.

ColorPipeline.title: ColorPipeline
ColorPipeline.description: The colour path from every source to the delivered file. Every field is required and none has a default: a colour decision a renderer supplies is invisible until print.
ColorPipeline.$comment:
THE ORDER OF OPERATIONS, ONCE, SO NEITHER SIDE INFERS IT (contracts#58)

  1. Decode each source. Geometry -- crop and scale -- is applied HERE, in the
     source's own encoding, before any colour conversion. Stated because
     scaling in linear light and scaling in a gamma-encoded space give
     different edges, and 'which one' must not be a renderer's habit.
  2. Linearise from that source's `MediaRef.color_encoding` into
     `working_space`, converting primaries by the chromatic-adaptation-free
     3x3 between the two primary sets, and scaling so 1.0 is reference white.
  3. Apply the clip's `color_ops`, in array order, as one fused matrix
     (see ColorOp).
  4. Apply `tone_map`, if present.
  5. Convert primaries to `output_encoding`'s and apply its transfer function.
     THIS is where values are clamped to [0,1], exactly once.
  6. Quantise to `EncodeProfile.video.pixel_format`.

A TRANSITION BLENDS AFTER ALL OF THIS, IN `output_encoding`. Both sides of a
dissolve or a dip have already reached step 5, so the blend weight mixes
delivered code values rather than linear light. Stated because the alternative
is defensible and different: blending in linear light is brighter through the
middle of every dissolve. It is also the only reading that is well defined when
the two sides come from sources with different encodings, since before step 5
they have no common value space at all.

THE IDENTITY CASE IS NORMATIVE, NOT AN OPTIMISATION.
When a source's `color_encoding` equals `output_encoding`, the clip carries no
`color_ops`, and `tone_map` is null, steps 2-5 MUST be skipped -- the code
values are passed through untouched. A round trip through linear light and back
is not lossless at 8 bits per channel; a renderer that inserted one would
change every frame of an ordinary SDR reel to no purpose, and the change would
be invisible in review and permanent in the file.

WHY input_transform IS GONE.
It was a single global string defaulting to "auto", which asked the renderer to
infer a transform from container metadata and said nothing about what to do
when that metadata was absent or wrong -- routine for action cameras and phone
HEVC. Worse, it was global: one plan can hold a phone's HLG clip and a DSLR's
BT.709 clip, and one string cannot describe both. The fact now lives per source
on `MediaRef.color_encoding`, stated by the planner from the MediaRecord that
ingest already probed. An untagged source is then a question the PLANNER
answers, once, in daylight -- not one the renderer answers per render.

working_space.description: Where colour ops and tone mapping compose. LINEAR-LIGHT RGB only, scaled so 1.0 is reference white -- the earlier enum mixed transfer names ('rec709') with 'linear' and with a log space, so it could not say what an op meant. `aces_cct` went with it: no worker here implements it, and its log curve has constants nothing in this repo states.

output_encoding.description: What the delivered file's code values mean, and what its container-level colour tags must say. SDR only at v0 -- see the ColorEncoding $comment.

tone_map.description: Required exactly when at least one source's `color_encoding` is an HDR member (bt2100_pq, bt2100_hlg); must be null otherwise. Checked as `color_pipeline_resolves`.

strategy.description: What was varied. Variants must differ along a stated axis, so the user's pick is interpretable as a preference rather than as noise.

description.description: One line the variant picker shows: 'faster, more action'.

EdlValidation.title: EdlValidation
EdlValidation.description: Result of the pre-render checks. The renderer refuses an EDL that has not passed, which keeps 'the renderer is dumb' from meaning 'the renderer is trusting'.

OtioExportInfo.title: OtioExportInfo
OtioExportInfo.description: Bookkeeping for the OTIO round trip. `unmapped_fields` must be empty for an export to be called lossless; if it is not, the exporter is telling us exactly which part of the contract has outgrown the mapping.

round_trip_verified.description: Set by the exporter after re-importing its own output and comparing to the source EDL. The claim of losslessness is tested per export, not assumed.
